title: Citi Cuts US Stocks After AI Rout, Finds a Safer Bet in Europe - The Wealth Advisor
text: Citigroup has downgraded US equities and global technology stocks following last week's AI-driven market rout, shifting its preference toward Europe as concerns about regulation and the enormous investment required to sustain the artificial intelligence boom unsettle Wall Street. The move, led by strategist Beata Manthey, follows the S&P 500's worst weekly decline since April 2025 and a staggering $2.3 trillion wipeout in the Nasdaq 100 last Thursday alone. Europe's Stoxx 600, meanwhile, managed a 0.2% gain, offering a glimpse of what happens when the market's biggest source of excitement becomes its biggest vulnerability. Citi reduced its US equity and global technology recommendations from overweight to neutral while raising European stocks, excluding the UK, to overweight. The bank remains optimistic about artificial intelligence over the longer term, but Manthey believes the selling could continue before investor positioning and earnings expectations find firmer ground. "We worry that positioning on key indices, such as the Nasdaq, could reset lower into net-short territory," Manthey wrote in a client note. The weakness has already spread beyond technology, suggesting that investors are reconsidering risks that looked manageable when AI enthusiasm was carrying the broader market. The immediate catalyst was last week's Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections, which heightened concerns that tougher regulation could slow construction of the data centers underpinning the AI expansion. Worries about the cost of financing that infrastructure were already building, leaving investors particularly sensitive to anything that might interrupt the industry's extraordinary spending plans. Europe offers something the US market increasingly lacks: relative independence from the AI trade. Its greater exposure to industrial companies, banks and defensive businesses once made European equities look comparatively unexciting, particularly when American technology giants were delivering much of the world's stock market appreciation. That disadvantage is becoming an advantage. Goldman Sachs strategists, including Guillaume Jaisson, have reached a similar conclusion, pointing to the enormous difference in how much the two markets depend on AI-related businesses. AI infrastructure accounts for roughly 15% of Europe's Stoxx 600, compared with approximately 40% of the S&P 500. The earnings comparison is even more striking. AI infrastructure companies represent less than one-quarter of the 9% earnings growth Goldman expects for the European benchmark in 2027, but more than two-thirds of projected US earnings growth. Europe's relative insulation has already proved valuable during previous reversals. Goldman found that European equities outperformed American stocks during all eight of the largest AI-driven selloffs since 2023, a remarkable record for a market that spent much of the technology boom struggling to keep pace. Citi also sees Europe benefiting more from declining oil prices, another potential advantage as investors reconsider the geographic distribution of their equity exposure. Lower energy costs could provide additional support to European businesses without requiring the kind of extraordinary capital spending that has become central to American technology valuations. Manthey's team is not abandoning risk altogether. Its global sector strategy now combines economically sensitive businesses with defensive holdings, and Citi has upgraded healthcare to overweight alongside materials. Nor has the bank turned outright bearish on equities. Its targets remain positive for next year, supported by expectations for lower interest rates, resilient economic conditions and potentially diminished geopolitical risks. The more consequential change is where Citi wants to take that risk. For years, American equities commanded a premium because their largest companies dominated the technologies expected to drive future earnings growth. That concentration rewarded investors handsomely as long as expectations kept rising. Now the same concentration leaves US stocks unusually exposed to questions about regulation, financing and whether AI investment can deliver the profits already embedded in valuations. Europe doesn't have to win the artificial intelligence race to benefit from that uncertainty. It may simply have to depend less on the outcome.
